Solar Scammer

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We meet the unhappy victims of a Solar installation scam - who've spent hundreds of thousands of rands to get their houses off the Eskom grid, only to be left with empty promises and empty pockets.

Unique Selling Point:
Jonathan Stephenson is the man behind a company called Solar Bay PTY LTD. They offer Solar installations to homes in both Cape Town and Johannesburg. But after getting paid large deposits from his clients, Stephenson simply fails to deliver on his promises.

Summary:
Stephenson works on a 50% deposit, and 35% payment on commencement of work basis. Which means that he gets 85% of his quote paid upfront. After receiving a 50% deposit, he'll arrive at his clients house with a few Solar panels - most of these are relatively cheap, and proceed to start installation. This gets his clients to fork over the further 35% of the cost as work has commenced. But once he's done that, Stephenson never returns to complete the Solar installation. He never delivers on the more expensive part of the installation, namely the inverter, batteries and electrical installation needed.
Our case studies in short:

Alberto Da Silva from JHB paid R171 931 up front in Septemeber 2020. To date he has only received a few solar panels. Da Silva has laid charges of fraud against Stephenson.

Maria Singh from JHB paid R161 000 in December 2020. To date she has only received 14 of 18 Solar panels and nothing else. Took Stephenson to court and got default judgement against him, but he has nothing to attach.

Charl Du Toit from Capte Town paid R140 000 in Feb 2020. In March received solar panels. In August 2021 went to the cops and laid charges. Stephenson then delivered the inverter. Du Toit is still waiting for the battery, a 10 kilowatt lithium one worth nearly R100 000. Stephenson keeps making promises.



Further information:
Stephenson has also been arrested previously for contempt of court. In his previous company We Drill Africa he had the same M.O. After his client Rosemary de la Harpe took him to court and got judgement against him, he hid his assets from the Sherrif of the court. He was then arrested. Rosemary, and her lawyer Werner Bock, are willing to do interviews. Werner Bock has been difficult to get a date set down as he is in high court on a big case, but has agreed to speak to me on the 13th of September. He has not given me de la Harpe's contact details yet, but has confirmed on email that she will speak to us.

Wynand has agreed that we set up a sting in Cape Town for Stephenson, as that is where he is based. We will phone him and ask him to do a quote for a house there. When he arrives we will confront him with the allegations. WG says if Stephenson says we are being unfair or have not given him enough time to prepare, we can give him written response or zoom.



Extra Budget Items:
Flights from JHB to Cape Town for producer and presenter. We do not have to stay over. Car rental for one day.

Script:


Solar Scammer
First Draft Script
21 September 2021



Voice
It’s an all too familiar scene for most South Africans - one minute you’re relaxing at home enjoying your favourite television program, and the next you’re stuck in the dark with no electricity…

Link Macfarlane
Load-shedding, power interruptions and Eskom in a near state of constant crisis, it’s become a part of our daily lives. So for those who can afford it, going off the grid with a decent solar system at your home makes a lot of sense. But buyer beware; wherever there’s a demand for a product, there’s also a lot of unscrupulous suppliers trying to make a quick buck.

Voice
In layman’s terms, these systems use Solar panels to convert sunlight into electricity. The electricity is stored in large batteries like these. The batteries feed into inverters, which convert the current to match your home’s power supply.

Last year Maria Singh from Johannesburg came across a company called Solar Bay, who were offering home solar systems.

Sound Up Maria
So I went on-line, checked them out on-line, and it looked good.

Voice
She got through to Jonathan Stephenson, the man whose cellphone number featured prominently on the landing page of the Solar Bay website.

Sound Up Maria
Maria: and he said to me I’m going to send you my manager’s number, Themba, because I’m in Cape Town, Themba works in Johannesburg.

Voice
She says their website made it seem like they were a large firm, with offices listed in both Cape Town and Johannesburg, even sporting a national sales hotline. According to the Companies and Intellectual Property Commission, or CIPC, Themba Tsotetsi is the sole director of Solar Bay, although Jonathan Stephenson seemed to be the man in charge.

Sound Up Maria
He said Themba’s the manager, and he was the owner.

Link Mac
Today’s solar systems are pretty hi-tec, you could provide your whole house with electricity, and even monitor everything that’s happening through an app like this one. But they don’t come cheap, costs could run into the hundreds of thousands of rands.

Voice
On the 1st of December last year, Singh received an email from Jonathan Stephenson confirming that he still had stock available for the 10kw system she and her husband had enquired about. He also attached a quotation for R195 500, 50% of which was payable upfront.

Sound Up Maria
So I paid the 50% 1st of December.
Voice
After she paid R97 500 as a deposit, it took more than two weeks for Solar Bay to finally arrive on site.

Sound Up Maria
The panels arrived,they were put on, instead of 18 panels I got 14. And then Themba said to me, he came at the end of the day and he said to me well if you want the battery and inverters by monday, because that was the friday, you need to pay the 35%.

Voice
According to the Solar Bay payment terms, clients have to pay a 50% deposit, an additional 35% on arrival on site, and 15% on completion.

Sound Up Maria
Maria: So we paid the 35%, expecting him to come on Monday with the batteries and inverter. And that’s when the whole run around started.

Voice
Despite paying 85% of the quoted price upfront, Singh never received the outstanding batteries and inverters.

Sound Up Maria
Mac: So what did you end up paying in total?

Maria: A hundred and sixty six thousand.

Mac: A hundred and sixty six, that’s a lot of money?

Maria: It’s a lot, lot of money you know.

Voice
Alberto da Silva also ordered a solar system from Stephenson in September last year. Just like Singh, he says he also paid Solar Bay R171 931 up front, but a whole year later all he’s ever received are these solar panels. No batteries, no inverters, no working solar system.

Sound Up Alberto Da Silva
Lots of promises, and lots of excuses. Truck broke down, he had a fall out with Themba, he said it’s Covid and the team that were going to do the installations got ill, he sent me a photograph of himself getting tested, he got robbed… All sorts of excuses.

Voice
da Silva has calculated the value of the work done to date at R45 000, leaving him out of pocket to the tune of R126 000. But Kelly Nel from Richardsbay says he’s never received a single thing from Solar Bay. And that after he also paid a R90 000 deposit in September last year.

Sound Up Kelly Nel
Mac: And would you say they’ve delivered?

Kelly: No, nothing, nothing. No batteries, no solar panels, nobody on site. I have not received anything from them, no one has even been out to my house to inspect it.






Link Mac
So we were skeptical about whether Stephenson would give us an on-camera interview, so our producer phoned him, pretending to be a client and asked him to come and give us a quotation at a house we’d leant here, in Cape Town.

Sound Up Jonathan Stephenson Phone Call
Producer: Are you guys from Solar Bay?

Jonathan: Yes.

Producer: Who am I speaking to?

Jonathan: It’s Jonathan.

Link Mac
After initially confirming that he was from Solar Bay, Stephenson suddenly changed his story saying that he now worked for a new company.

Sound Up Jonathan Stephenson Phone Call
Jonathan: To be honest with you we sort of have stopped with the Solar Bay side, because I sort of tried to pull out of the company, ha ha ha, but I keep this phone on because obviously, I’ve got people who phone me for technical side.

Voice
Perhaps it had something to do with all the negative publicity the company was getting online. Meanwhile, Stephenson told our undercover producer the new company was called Hello Solar, and said that they outsourced work to him.

Sound Up Jonathan Stephenson Phone Call
Jonathan: So I basically took my team, and then like I work under them now.

Producer: Ok

Jonathan: For the next couple of months, because they’re doing some… they outsource some work to our side.

Voice
Intrigued, we did a little more digging. The Hello Solar website also boasted offices in Cape Town and Johannesburg. We took a hidden camera to their Cape Town address, and found out it was only a “virtual” office…

Sound Up Hidden Camera
Woman: They have a virtual office, so no they’re not physically here, they just have an address, a telephone number, and we can receive packages for them..

Mac: Oh ok so but there’s no one in the office, there’s no one here?

Lady: No.

Voice
We hit another brick wall with the CIPC, since Hello Solar does not show up on their database as a registered company. But then we had a breakthrough after we downloaded a quotation from the Hello Solar website. And although it didn’t show a company registration number, it did have a VAT number…

Link Mac
That VAT number for Hello Solar is, Ke Tsona Tobacco. But guess who’s the owner of Ke Tsona Tobacco?

Voice
No prizes for guessing Jonathan Stephenson. Both Stephenson and Tsotetsi have been joint directors in at least 6 other companies we know of. Armed with the new information, we were preparing for Stephenson to arrive at the house in Cape Town, when he called our producer to cancel the appointment.

Sound Up Jonathan
Sorry man I don’t think I’m going to be able to make it, there’s too much to do, to like sort out here…

Voice
A few days later, we phoned Stephenson to ask him for an interview.

Sound Up Jonathan Phone Call
Mac: We obviously have to give you a right of reply Jonathan, would you be willing to do an on camera interview with us?

Jonathan: I really don’t want to be on Carte Blanche, for what man? I’m fixing it up, I’m like two weeks away from everyone being finished.

Voice
But Maria Singh is still waiting for a refund, after she eventually took Solar Bay to court.

Sound Up Maria
Well we issued a summons, and they didn’t respond to it. And we got a default judgment from the Randburg court. We also went to the police, we laid a charge of theft and fraud.

Voice
It’s not the first time Stephenson has ended up in court for taking money from clients and not delivering. He’s also had two judgments against him and his former company We Drill Africa, where he failed to dig boreholes for his clients.

With Solar Bay, Stephenson blamed his suppliers for many of his woes. At first he said it was a company who’d closed down.

Sound Up Jonathan Phone Call
Mac: If somebody gives you a R170 000 and has to wait for a year, I’d be pretty, pretty irate?

Jonathan: Ja no I do take that point, but I can only go as quickly as I can go to sort it out. We also got taken for money. Ok, not taken, but they closed down.

Voice
But in this later phone call to our producer, who had by now identified himself as a journalist, Stephenson’s story changed again. This time he said a mysterious man they allegedly met outside a suppliers warehouse, had failed to deliver stock they’d paid him for in cash.

Sound Up Jonathan Phone Call
Producer: And you paid him upfront and then he never delivered?

Jonathan: yeah, yeah.

Producer: Who is this person?

Jonathan: Well, to this day we don’t know. We got panels from him, and no machines. And we met him outside, and that’s where we landed up, that’s where our mistake came.

Link Mac
We were all setup and ready to hear Jonathan and Themba’s side of the story in an on camera interview later on today, an interview we’d given them a whole week’s chance to prepare for. But then the phone rang, and our earlier doubts about him actually agreeing to come on camera, were confirmed.

Voice
Themba Tsotetsi said he wanted to consult with a lawyer.

Sound Up Jonathan Phone Call
Jonathan: You can tell him that we obviously want to meet with the lawyer.

Themba: Ja I would like to meet with my lawyer, and I’m literally about two weeks from completion in terms of getting everything sorted, as to what is outstanding to the customers.

Producer: You know what the pity is, sorry to interrupt you, you guys have known for a week now, you agreed to it, now again it’s an excuse you know. So it sounds like it’s just excuses upon excuses which you’ve been giving your own clients also

Jonathan: I did tell you that on tuesday we’re two weeks away, you know.

Producer: it’s a year later for most of them, and for some of them even longer than a year. So now that the media is speaking to you now you want to fix it?

Jonathan: We’ve been fixing it, we’ve been fixing it the whole time.

Voice
But three weeks after we first contacted Solar Bay, Kelly Nel and Maria Singh are still waiting. Alberto da Silva has received one inverter, but without the batteries and installation, it’s not been much use during this week’s national load-shedding.

Sound Up Alberto
Im going to call him Mr Excuses, I mean, you know…

Voice
When we asked Stephenson who owned Hello Solar, his story changed again.

Sound Up Jonathan Phone Call
Producer: the VAT number on the Hello Solar letterhead goes to Ke Tsona?

Jonathan: Yes, that’s exactly correct.

Producer: Which is a company you’re a director of?

Jonathan: Yes, that’s correct. And I’ve got three other partners now that have backed, to get it.

Producer: So you are the owner of Hello Solar?

Jonathan: We, we’re one of the partners yes.

Voice
In a follow up letter, Stephenson and Tsotetsi reiterated that they were let down by suppliers, and also said: “Coupled with Covid-19 and a disastrous supply chain it is better described as having destroyed our business, our personal lives, and our reputations and more importantly, has hurt our clients. We ask forgiveness from our clients.”

But da Silva says he would prefer a working solar system to an apology.

Sound Up Alberto
It sounds like he’s trying to setup another one of these businesses, and he’s not even satisfying the customers that he’s got.

Voice
Stephenson also acknowledged the lawsuits against We Drill Africa, and said: “I pay them as per the court order every month”. But the Solar Bay experience has been a bitter pill to swallow for Maria Singh, who has since paid even more money to a new supplier to finish her solar system. And in case you’re wondering, it took all of two days.

Sound Up Maria
So I was really angry, because it was a huge amount of money, that I’ve just handed over to someone, who I you know, trusted blindly. And now I’m hesitant to hand over even one rand to anyone, who’s going to do any kind of work at my house.

Voice
Despite again missing their promised two-week-deadline of sorting out their clients, Stephenson is adamant they will deliver.


Link Macfarlane
The question is do you believe him?

END

A year after forking out hundreds of thousands of rands, one solar installation company’s customer’s say they’re still waiting for the goods… (9sec)

Sound Up Maria
Mac: So what did you end up paying in total?

Maria: A hundred and sixty six thousand.

Mac: A hundred and sixty six, that’s a lot of money… (6sec)

We investigate solar installations gone wrong

Sound Up Alberto Da Silva
Lots of promises, and lots of excuses.







Promo 2 (21 sec)

Voice
Imagine paying for a solar system in your home, and a year later still not having the goods. (6sec)

Sound Up Mac
It’s more like slowly, some of these people have even gone so far as opening up cases against you at the SAPS. (5sec)

Voice
We investigate a man whose clients are calling him Mr Excuses. (5sec)

Sound Up Alberto
Im going to call him Mr Excuses, I mean, you know… (4sec)




Promo 3 (11 sec)
We investigate a company accused of reneging on their promises to clients who thought they were buying their dream solar systems. But after handing over their cash, many of them have been left in the lurch.

Link Mac So we were skeptical about whether Stephenson would give us an on-camera interview, so our producer phoned him, pretending to be a client and asked him to come and give us a quotation at a house we’d leant here, in Cape Town. Sound Up Jonathan Stephenson Phone Call Producer: Are you guys from Solar Bay? Jonathan: Yes. Producer: Who am I speaking to? Jonathan: It’s Jonathan. Link Mac After initially confirming that he was from Solar Bay, Stephenson suddenly changed his story saying that he now worked for a new company. Sound Up Jonathan Stephenson Phone Call Jonathan: To be honest with you we sort of have stopped with the Solar Bay side, because I sort of tried to pull out of the company, ha ha ha, but I keep this phone on because obviously, I’ve got people who phone me for technical side. Voice Perhaps it had something to do with all the negative publicity the company was getting online. Meanwhile, Stephenson told our undercover producer the new company was called Hello Solar, and said that they outsourced work to him. Sound Up Jonathan Stephenson Phone Call Jonathan: So I basically took my team, and then like I work under them now. Producer: Ok Jonathan: For the next couple of months, because they’re doing some… they outsource some work to our side. Voice Intrigued, we did a little more digging. The Hello Solar website also boasted offices in Cape Town and Johannesburg. We took a hidden camera to their Cape Town address, and found out it was only a “virtual” office… Sound Up Hidden Camera Woman: They have a virtual office, so no they’re not physically here, they just have an address, a telephone number, and we can receive packages for them.. Mac: Oh ok so but there’s no one in the office, there’s no one here? Lady: No. Voice We hit another brick wall with the CIPC, since Hello Solar does not show up on their database as a registered company. But then we had a breakthrough after we downloaded a quotation from the Hello Solar website. And although it didn’t show a company registration number, it did have a VAT number… Link Mac That VAT number for Hello Solar is, Ke Tsona Tobacco. But guess who’s the owner of Ke Tsona Tobacco? Voice No prizes for guessing Jonathan Stephenson. Both Stephenson and Tsotetsi have been joint directors in at least 6 other companies we know of. Armed with the new information, we were preparing for Stephenson to arrive at the house in Cape Town, when he called our producer to cancel the appointment. Sound Up Jonathan Sorry man I don’t think I’m going to be able to make it, there’s too much to do, to like sort out here… Voice A few days later, we phoned Stephenson to ask him for an interview. Sound Up Jonathan Phone Call Mac: We obviously have to give you a right of reply Jonathan, would you be willing to do an on camera interview with us? Jonathan: I really don’t want to be on Carte Blanche, for what man? I’m fixing it up, I’m like two weeks away from everyone being finished. Voice But Maria Singh is still waiting for a refund, after she eventually took Solar Bay to court. Sound Up Maria Well we issued a summons, and they didn’t respond to it. And we got a default judgment from the Randburg court. We also went to the police, we laid a charge of theft and fraud. Voice It’s not the first time Stephenson has ended up in court for taking money from clients and not delivering. He’s also had two judgments against him and his former company We Drill Africa, where he failed to dig boreholes for his clients. With Solar Bay, Stephenson blamed his suppliers for many of his woes. At first he said it was a company who’d closed down. Sound Up Jonathan Phone Call Mac: If somebody gives you a R170 000 and has to wait for a year, I’d be pretty, pretty irate? Jonathan: Ja no I do take that point, but I can only go as quickly as I can go to sort it out. We also got taken for money. Ok, not taken, but they closed down. Voice But in this later phone call to our producer, who had by now identified himself as a journalist, Stephenson’s story changed again. This time he said a mysterious man they allegedly met outside a suppliers warehouse, had failed to deliver stock they’d paid him for in cash. Sound Up Jonathan Phone Call Producer: And you paid him upfront and then he never delivered? Jonathan: yeah, yeah. Producer: Who is this person? Jonathan: Well, to this day we don’t know. We got panels from him, and no machines. And we met him outside, and that’s where we landed up, that’s where our mistake came. Link Mac We were all setup and ready to hear Jonathan and Themba’s side of the story in an on camera interview later on today, an interview we’d given them a whole week’s chance to prepare for. But then the phone rang, and our earlier doubts about him actually agreeing to come on camera, were confirmed. Voice Themba Tsotetsi said he wanted to consult with a lawyer. Sound Up Jonathan Phone Call Jonathan: You can tell him that we obviously want to meet with the lawyer. Themba: Ja I would like to meet with my lawyer, and I’m literally about two weeks from completion in terms of getting everything sorted, as to what is outstanding to the customers. Producer: You know what the pity is, sorry to interrupt you, you guys have known for a week now, you agreed to it, now again it’s an excuse you know. So it sounds like it’s just excuses upon excuses which you’ve been giving your own clients also Jonathan: I did tell you that on tuesday we’re two weeks away, you know. Producer: it’s a year later for most of them, and for some of them even longer than a year. So now that the media is speaking to you now you want to fix it? Jonathan: We’ve been fixing it, we’ve been fixing it the whole time. Voice But three weeks after we first contacted Solar Bay, Kelly Nel and Maria Singh are still waiting. Alberto da Silva has received one inverter, but without the batteries and installation, it’s not been much use during this week’s national load-shedding. Sound Up Alberto Im going to call him Mr Excuses, I mean, you know… Voice When we asked Stephenson who owned Hello Solar, his story changed again. Sound Up Jonathan Phone Call Producer: the VAT number on the Hello Solar letterhead goes to Ke Tsona? Jonathan: Yes, that’s exactly correct. Producer: Which is a company you’re a director of? Jonathan: Yes, that’s correct. And I’ve got three other partners now that have backed, to get it. Producer: So you are the owner of Hello Solar? Jonathan: We, we’re one of the partners yes. Voice In a follow up letter, Stephenson and Tsotetsi reiterated that they were let down by suppliers, and also said: “Coupled with Covid-19 and a disastrous supply chain it is better described as having destroyed our business, our personal lives, and our reputations and more importantly, has hurt our clients. We ask forgiveness from our clients.” But da Silva says he would prefer a working solar system to an apology. Sound Up Alberto It sounds like he’s trying to setup another one of these businesses, and he’s not even satisfying the customers that he’s got. Voice Stephenson also acknowledged the lawsuits against We Drill Africa, and said: “I pay them as per the court order every month”. But the Solar Bay experience has been a bitter pill to swallow for Maria Singh, who has since paid even more money to a new supplier to finish her solar system. And in case you’re wondering, it took all of two days. Sound Up Maria So I was really angry, because it was a huge amount of money, that I’ve just handed over to someone, who I you know, trusted blindly. And now I’m hesitant to hand over even one rand to anyone, who’s going to do any kind of work at my house. Voice Despite again missing their promised two-week-deadline of sorting out their clients, Stephenson is adamant they will deliver. Link Macfarlane The question is do you believe him? END Promos Promo1 (21 sec) Voice A year after forking out hundreds of thousands of rands, one solar installation company’s customer’s say they’re still waiting for the goods… (9sec) Sound Up Maria Mac: So what did you end up paying in total? Maria: A hundred and sixty six thousand. Mac: A hundred and sixty six, that’s a lot of money… (6sec) Voice We investigate solar installations gone wrong Sound Up Alberto Da Silva Lots of promises, and lots of excuses. Promo 2 (21 sec) Voice Imagine paying for a solar system in your home, and a year later still not having the goods. (6sec) Sound Up Mac It’s more like slowly, some of these people have even gone so far as opening up cases against you at the SAPS. (5sec) Voice We investigate a man whose clients are calling him Mr Excuses. (5sec) Sound Up Alberto Im going to call him Mr Excuses, I mean, you know… (4sec) Promo 3 (11 sec) We investigate a company accused of reneging on their promises to clients who thought they were buying their dream solar systems. But after handing over their cash, many of them have been left in the lurch.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We meet the unhappy victims of a Solar installation scam - who've spent hundreds of thousands of rands to get their houses off the Eskom grid, only to be left with empty promises and empty pockets.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Jonathan Stephenson is the man behind a company called Solar Bay PTY LTD. They offer Solar installations to homes in both Cape Town and Johannesburg. But after getting paid large deposits from his clients, Stephenson simply fails to deliver on his promises.
metadata.Summary: Stephenson works on a 50% deposit, and 35% payment on commencement of work basis. Which means that he gets 85% of his quote paid upfront. After receiving a 50% deposit, he'll arrive at his clients house with a few Solar panels - most of these are relatively cheap, and proceed to start installation. This gets his clients to fork over the further 35% of the cost as work has commenced. But once he's done that, Stephenson never returns to complete the Solar installation. He never delivers on the more expensive part of the installation, namely the inverter, batteries and electrical installation needed. Our case studies in short: Alberto Da Silva from JHB paid R171 931 up front in Septemeber 2020. To date he has only received a few solar panels. Da Silva has laid charges of fraud against Stephenson. Maria Singh from JHB paid R161 000 in December 2020. To date she has only received 14 of 18 Solar panels and nothing else. Took Stephenson to court and got default judgement against him, but he has nothing to attach. Charl Du Toit from Capte Town paid R140 000 in Feb 2020. In March received solar panels. In August 2021 went to the cops and laid charges. Stephenson then delivered the inverter. Du Toit is still waiting for the battery, a 10 kilowatt lithium one worth nearly R100 000. Stephenson keeps making promises.
metadata.Further information: Stephenson has also been arrested previously for contempt of court. In his previous company We Drill Africa he had the same M.O. After his client Rosemary de la Harpe took him to court and got judgement against him, he hid his assets from the Sherrif of the court. He was then arrested. Rosemary, and her lawyer Werner Bock, are willing to do interviews. Werner Bock has been difficult to get a date set down as he is in high court on a big case, but has agreed to speak to me on the 13th of September. He has not given me de la Harpe's contact details yet, but has confirmed on email that she will speak to us. Wynand has agreed that we set up a sting in Cape Town for Stephenson, as that is where he is based. We will phone him and ask him to do a quote for a house there. When he arrives we will confront him with the allegations. WG says if Stephenson says we are being unfair or have not given him enough time to prepare, we can give him written response or zoom.
metadata.Extra Budget Items: Flights from JHB to Cape Town for producer and presenter. We do not have to stay over. Car rental for one day.
